shopping-01.meaning: Asking where a product is in the shop.
shopping-01.order: A question word takes the first position, so the finite verb comes second, then the subject. The second verb (the infinitive) goes to the very end, after the object.
shopping-01.forms: Kunnen is irregular: ik kan, jij kunt or kan, wij kunnen. Melk is a de-word: de melk.
shopping-01.compare: English also puts "can" before "I", but keeps "find" next to the subject. Dutch sends the infinitive to the end.

mistake.wrong: Waar ik kan de melk vinden?
mistake.right: Waar kan ik de melk vinden?
mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

shopping-02.order: A main clause has the subject first and the finite verb second. Graag comes after the verb and softens the wish; alstublieft ends the request without changing the order.
shopping-02.forms: Willen: ik wil, jij wilt, u wilt. Broodjes is the plural of het broodje (the -je ending makes it a het-word).
shopping-02.compare: English says "I would like"; Dutch uses the plain present ik wil plus graag to be just as polite.

mistake.why: The finite verb stays second; graag follows it.

shopping-03.meaning: Asking whether you can pay by card.
shopping-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kan), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (betalen) goes to the end.
shopping-03.forms: Kan ik: ik kan. Kaart is a de-word: de kaart.
shopping-03.compare: English keeps "pay" next to "I"; Dutch puts betalen last, after the manner phrase.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan met de kaart betalen?
mistake.right: Kan ik met de kaart betalen?
mistake.why: A yes/no question puts the finite verb first.

shopping-04.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoeveel) takes the first position, so the finite verb (kost) comes second and the subject (deze tas) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
shopping-04.forms: Kosten: het kost, ze kosten. Tas is a de-word, so deze (a het-word would take dit).
shopping-04.compare: English needs "does" in the question; Dutch just moves the verb forward.

mistake.why: Tas is a de-word, so use deze, not dit.

shopping-05.meaning: Asking whether the shop has a smaller size too.
shopping-05.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heeft), and the subject (u) follows it.
shopping-05.forms: U takes the same verb form as hij: u heeft (u hebt is also correct). Kleinere is kleiner plus -e: after een with a de-word (maat) the adjective takes -e.
shopping-05.compare: English uses "do you have"; Dutch simply inverts heeft and u.

mistake.wrong: Heeft u ook een kleiner maat?
mistake.right: Heeft u ook een kleinere maat?
mistake.why: Maat is a de-word, so the adjective takes -e after een.

shopping-06.meaning: Telling the cashier you do not need a bag.
shopping-06.order: A main clause: subject, then finite verb. Nodig completes the expression nodig hebben and goes to the end.
shopping-06.forms: Hebben: ik heb. Geen replaces een in a negative sentence: een zak becomes geen zak.
shopping-06.compare: English says "I do not need a bag"; Dutch uses geen plus the noun, with no "do".

mistake.wrong: Ik heb niet een zak nodig.
mistake.why: Use geen instead of niet een before a noun.

shopping-07.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it.
shopping-07.forms: Mogen: ik mag, jij mag, wij mogen. Bon is a de-word.
shopping-07.compare: English says "May I have the receipt?"; Dutch usually drops the final verb.

mistake.why: Put the finite verb first to ask permission.

shopping-08.meaning: Saying that these apples cost less.
shopping-08.order: A main clause with the subject first and the finite verb second. After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
shopping-08.forms: A plural subject needs zijn, not is. Goedkoper is goedkoop plus -er.
shopping-08.compare: English forms the comparative with -er too ("cheaper").

mistake.why: A plural subject takes zijn.

shopping-09.meaning: Saying what gift you are looking for.
shopping-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zoek) second (verb-second order).
shopping-09.forms: Zoeken: ik zoek. Mijn does not change before de- or het-words. Cadeau is a het-word.
shopping-09.compare: English says "I am looking for"; Dutch uses the simple present ik zoek.

mistake.why: Dutch uses the simple present here, not ben plus an infinitive.

shopping-10.meaning: Telling the seller which item you will take.
shopping-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (neem) second (verb-second order).
shopping-10.forms: Nemen: ik neem. Deze stands for a de-word or plural you are pointing at; a het-word needs dit.
shopping-10.compare: English says "I'll take this one"; Dutch uses the plain present for an immediate decision.

mistake.why: Tas is a de-word, so use deze.

school-01.meaning: Politely asking a teacher to explain something again.
school-01.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunt), and the subject (u) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (uitleggen) goes to the end.
school-01.forms: Kunnen with u: u kunt (u kan is also used). Uitleggen is a separable verb but stays whole after a modal.
school-01.compare: English says "Can you explain that again?"; the word order is similar but the Dutch infinitive is last.

mistake.wrong: U kunt dat nog eens uitleggen?
mistake.right: Kunt u dat nog eens uitleggen?
mistake.why: Put the finite verb first to ask the question.

school-02.meaning: Saying you do not understand a question.
school-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (begrijp) second (verb-second order).
school-02.forms: Begrijpen: ik begrijp (the prefix be- means no ge- in the participle: begrepen). Vraag is a de-word, so deze.
school-02.compare: English says "I do not understand"; Dutch has no "do", just niet at the end.

mistake.why: Niet normally comes after the object, not before the verb.

school-03.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (betekent) comes second and the subject (dit woord) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
school-03.forms: Betekenen: het betekent. Woord is a het-word, so dit.
school-03.compare: English says "What does this word mean?" with "does"; Dutch has no auxiliary here.

mistake.why: Woord is a het-word, so use dit.

school-04.meaning: Politely asking if you may ask something quickly.
school-04.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vragen) goes to the end.
school-04.forms: Mogen: ik mag. Even softens the request ("for a moment").
school-04.compare: English says "May I ask something quickly?"; the same inversion, but Dutch puts the infinitive last.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb.

school-05.meaning: Saying you have already done your homework.
school-05.order: In the perfect tense the auxiliary is the finite verb in second position and the participle goes to the end.
school-05.forms: Perfect = hebben plus participle: ik heb gemaakt. Mijn does not change.
school-05.compare: English says "I have already done"; Dutch also uses an auxiliary plus participle, but the participle is at the end.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb gemaakt mijn huiswerk al.
mistake.right: Ik heb mijn huiswerk al gemaakt.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end of the clause.

school-06.meaning: Asking when something must be handed in.
school-06.order: A question word first, then the finite verb, then the subject. The infinitive goes to the end.
school-06.forms: Moeten: wij moeten. Inleveren is separable (lever ... in), but it stays whole after a modal.
school-06.compare: English says "When do we have to hand this in?"; Dutch uses moeten plus an infinitive at the end.

mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

school-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Mijn pen) comes first and the finite verb (ligt) second (verb-second order).
school-07.forms: Liggen: het ligt. Op tafel has no article, which is normal in this fixed phrase (op de tafel is also possible).
school-07.compare: English just says "is"; Dutch tells how the object is placed: ligt, staat, zit.

mistake.why: Dutch prefers a position verb such as ligt for a pen lying down.

school-08.meaning: Saying where you are going tomorrow.
school-08.order: When a time word is first, the finite verb must still be second, so it comes before the subject (inversion).
school-08.forms: Gaan: ik ga. Naar school has no article.
school-08.compare: English also says "Tomorrow I am going", but English keeps the subject before the verb; Dutch must put the verb first.

mistake.why: After a fronted time word, the verb comes before the subject.

school-09.order: After omdat the clause is subordinate, so the finite verb goes to the very end. In the main clause the verb stays second.
school-09.forms: Zijn: ik ben. Vertraging hebben means to be delayed.
school-09.compare: English keeps the verb in the middle of the because-clause; Dutch moves it to the end.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn trein heeft vertraging.
mistake.right: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn trein vertraging heeft.
mistake.why: After omdat the finite verb goes to the end.

school-10.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (oefenen) goes to the end.
school-10.compare: English says "Can we practise together?"; the order is similar, but Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.why: Start a yes/no question with the finite verb.

transport-01.meaning: Asking which platform a train leaves from.
transport-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Van welk spoor) takes the first position, so the finite verb (vertrekt) comes second and the subject (de trein) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-01.forms: Vertrekken: de trein vertrekt. Welk goes with het-words (het spoor); welke with de-words.
transport-01.compare: English puts "from" at the end ("Which platform does it leave from?"); Dutch keeps Van welk spoor together at the front.

mistake.wrong: Welk spoor vertrekt de trein van?
mistake.right: Van welk spoor vertrekt de trein?
mistake.why: Keep the preposition with its noun at the front of the question.

transport-02.meaning: Asking if you have to change trains here.
transport-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Moet), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (overstappen) goes to the end.
transport-02.forms: Moeten: ik moet. In a main clause overstappen would split: ik stap over.
transport-02.compare: English says "Do I have to change here?"; Dutch uses moeten plus infinitive.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb.

transport-03.meaning: Asking if this train goes to Bruges.
transport-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Gaat), and the subject (deze trein) follows it.
transport-03.forms: Gaan: de trein gaat. Trein is a de-word, so deze.
transport-03.compare: English says "Does this train go to Bruges?" with "does"; Dutch only inverts.

mistake.why: Start with the finite verb to make a yes/no question.

transport-04.meaning: Politely asking for a ticket to a city.
transport-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order).
transport-04.forms: Willen: ik wil. Ticket is a het-word (een ticket).
transport-04.compare: English says "I would like"; Dutch uses the present ik wil.

mistake.wrong: Ik wil een ticket in Gent, alstublieft.
mistake.right: Ik wil een ticket naar Gent, alstublieft.
mistake.why: Use naar for the destination.

transport-05.meaning: Asking what time the train arrives.
transport-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe laat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (komt) comes second and the subject (de trein) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (aan) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-05.forms: Aankomen is separable: de trein komt ... aan.
transport-05.compare: English says "arrive" as one word; Dutch splits the verb in a main clause.

mistake.right: Hoe laat komt de trein aan?
mistake.why: A separable verb splits: the verb is second and the particle goes last.

transport-06.meaning: Asking if a seat is free.
transport-06.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (deze plaats) follows it.
transport-06.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e: vrij. Plaats is a de-word, so deze.
transport-06.compare: English says "Is this seat free?" with the same order.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb.

transport-07.meaning: Saying your train is delayed by ten minutes.
transport-07.order: A main clause: subject first, finite verb second. The duration comes before vertraging.
transport-07.forms: Hebben: de trein heeft. Vertraging hebben means to be delayed.
transport-07.compare: English says "is ten minutes late"; Dutch says "has ten minutes of delay".

mistake.wrong: Mijn trein is tien minuten vertraging.
mistake.right: Mijn trein heeft tien minuten vertraging.
mistake.why: Use heeft vertraging, not is vertraging.

transport-08.meaning: Asking where you can buy a ticket.
transport-08.order: A question word first, then the finite verb, then the subject. The infinitive goes to the end.
transport-08.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Ticket is a het-word.
transport-08.compare: English says "Where can I buy my ticket?"; the order is very similar.

mistake.wrong: Waar ik kan mijn ticket kopen?
mistake.right: Waar kan ik mijn ticket kopen?
mistake.why: In a question the finite verb comes before the subject.

transport-09.meaning: Saying where you will get off.
transport-09.order: A main clause: subject, finite verb, then the rest. The particle uit goes to the end.
transport-09.forms: Uitstappen is separable: ik stap ... uit. Volgende takes -e before the de-word halte.
transport-09.compare: English says "I get off"; Dutch splits stap and uit.

mistake.wrong: Ik uitstap bij de volgende halte.
mistake.right: Ik stap bij de volgende halte uit.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

transport-10.meaning: Politely asking for help with your luggage.
transport-10.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunt), and the subject (u) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (helpen) goes to the end.
transport-10.forms: Kunnen with u: u kunt. Mij is the object form of ik (me).
transport-10.compare: English says "Can you help me with my luggage?" with the same order.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u helpen mij met mijn bagage?
mistake.right: Kunt u mij helpen met mijn bagage?
mistake.why: Put the object before the infinitive.

home-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zijn) comes second and the subject (mijn sleutels) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
home-01.forms: Zijn agrees with the plural subject: sleutels zijn. Mijn does not change.
home-01.compare: English says "Where are my keys?" with the same order.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

home-02.meaning: Saying that you are busy cooking right now.
home-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (koken) goes to the end.
home-02.forms: Zijn: ik ben. After aan het the verb is an infinitive, not conjugated.
home-02.compare: English uses "-ing" (I am cooking); Dutch uses ben aan het koken.

mistake.why: The progressive needs aan het before the infinitive.

home-03.meaning: Asking if someone locked the door.
home-03.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedaan) goes to the end.
home-03.forms: Perfect: heb je gedaan. De deur op slot doen means to lock the door.
home-03.compare: English says "Have you locked the door?"; the participle is also late, but Dutch puts it at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Je hebt de deur op slot gedaan?
mistake.right: Heb je de deur op slot gedaan?
mistake.why: Put the auxiliary first to ask the question.

home-04.meaning: Saying you have already done the dishes.
home-04.order: In the perfect tense the auxiliary is second and the participle goes to the end.
home-04.forms: Perfect: ik heb gedaan. De afwas doen means to do the dishes.
home-04.compare: English says "I have already done the dishes"; Dutch puts the participle last.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb gedaan de afwas al.
mistake.right: Ik heb de afwas al gedaan.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

home-05.meaning: Asking someone to open the window.
home-05.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kun), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (openmaken) goes to the end.
home-05.forms: Kunnen with je: kun je (the -t drops after je). Raam is a het-word.
home-05.compare: English says "Can you open the window?"; the order is similar.

mistake.why: Put the finite verb first for a request.

home-06.meaning: Telling someone a cup is theirs.
home-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-06.forms: Zijn: dit is. Dit points to a het-word or to something in general.
home-06.compare: English says "This is your cup"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: The possessive is jouw (or je), not jou.

home-07.meaning: Saying you cycle home after work.
home-07.order: A time phrase first pushes the finite verb ahead of the subject (inversion), because the verb is always second.
home-07.forms: Fietsen: ik fiets. Naar huis means home.
home-07.compare: English keeps "I" before the verb; Dutch must put the verb second.

mistake.wrong: Na het werk ik fiets naar huis.
mistake.right: Na het werk fiets ik naar huis.
mistake.why: After a fronted time phrase, the verb comes before the subject.

home-08.meaning: Saying there is milk in the fridge.
home-08.order: Er comes first, the verb second, then the real subject. Dutch uses staat for things standing or placed somewhere.
home-08.forms: Staan: er staat. For plural things: Er staan appels in de koelkast.
home-08.compare: English says "There is"; Dutch says "There stands".

mistake.wrong: Er is melk in de koelkast.
mistake.right: Er staat melk in de koelkast.
mistake.why: Dutch often uses staat, ligt or zit instead of is.

home-09.meaning: Saying you are tidying your room.
home-09.order: A main clause: the verb is second and the separable particle op goes to the end.
home-09.compare: English says "I tidy up my room" with "up" next to the verb; Dutch puts op at the end.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

home-10.order: Zullen we plus an infinitive makes a suggestion. The question starts with the finite verb and ends with the infinitive.
home-10.compare: English says "Shall we eat together?"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: A suggestion starts with Zullen we.

conversation-01.meaning: Saying you speak a little Dutch.
conversation-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (spreek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-01.forms: Spreken: ik spreek, jij spreekt. A language name has no article.
conversation-01.compare: English says "a little Dutch"; Dutch says "a bit Dutch".

mistake.wrong: Ik spreek een beetje de Nederlands.
mistake.why: A language name takes no article.

conversation-02.meaning: Asking someone to speak a bit more slowly.
conversation-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kun), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (spreken) goes to the end.
conversation-02.forms: Kun je: the -t drops after je. Langzamer is the comparative of langzaam.
conversation-02.compare: English says "Can you speak more slowly?" with the adverb after "speak"; Dutch puts it before the infinitive.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-03.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe) takes the first position, so the finite verb (gaat) comes second and the subject (het) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-03.forms: Gaan: het gaat. Met je (informal) or met u (polite).
conversation-03.compare: English says "How are you?"; Dutch literally says "How goes it with you?".

mistake.why: Dutch uses gaat het met je for how someone is.

conversation-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (woon) second (verb-second order).
conversation-04.forms: Wonen: ik woon. Use in with towns.
conversation-04.compare: English says "I live in"; the order is the same.

mistake.why: Use in with towns and countries.

conversation-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (kom) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-05.forms: Komen: je komt, but the -t drops when je follows: kom je.
conversation-05.compare: English says "Where are you from?"; Dutch literally says "Where come you from?".

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject and the -t drops after je.

conversation-06.meaning: Asking if someone has time tomorrow.
conversation-06.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it.
conversation-06.forms: Heb je: the -t of hebt drops after je.
conversation-06.compare: English says "Do you have time tomorrow?" with "do".

mistake.why: Start a yes/no question with the finite verb.

conversation-07.order: A main clause: subject then finite verb. Niet comes before the infinitive at the end.
conversation-07.compare: English says "I cannot come today"; Dutch puts niet before komen.

mistake.why: Niet comes before the infinitive at the end.

conversation-08.order: A suggestion starts with Zullen we, and the infinitive goes to the end.
conversation-08.forms: Om drie uur gives a clock time. Afspreken stays whole after zullen.
conversation-08.compare: English says "Shall we meet at three?"; Dutch uses the verb afspreken (arrange to meet).

mistake.wrong: Zullen we om drie uur spreken af?
mistake.right: Zullen we om drie uur afspreken?
mistake.why: After a modal the separable verb stays whole: afspreken.

conversation-09.meaning: Saying you are tired but feel good.
conversation-09.order: Maar joins two main clauses, so each keeps its own verb in second position.
conversation-09.forms: Zich voelen: ik voel me. After zijn and voelen the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-09.compare: English says "I feel good"; Dutch needs the reflexive me.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben moe, maar ik voel goed.
mistake.right: Ik ben moe, maar ik voel me goed.
mistake.why: Voelen is reflexive here: ik voel me.

conversation-10.order: This is a short phrase with no finite verb, so there is no verb-second order to follow: bedankt comes first and voor introduces what you are thanking someone for.
conversation-10.forms: Je means your before a noun (je hulp).
conversation-10.compare: English says "Thanks for your help"; Dutch uses voor too.

mistake.why: Bedankt voor introduces what you are thanking someone for.

conversation-11.meaning: Saying someone is worried about losing his keys.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: over het verliezen van zijn sleutels

conversation-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (maakt) second (verb-second order).
conversation-11.forms: The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: ik maak me, jij maakt je, hij maakt zich, wij maken ons. Het verliezen is an infinitive used as a noun.
conversation-11.compare: English says "He worries about losing"; Dutch uses zich zorgen maken over.

mistake.wrong: Hij maakt me zorgen over zijn sleutels.
mistake.right: Hij maakt zich zorgen over zijn sleutels.
mistake.why: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject (hij ... zich).

administration-01.meaning: Asking for the current exchange rate.
administration-01.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de huidige wisselkoers) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
administration-01.forms: Huidige takes -e because it follows the article de. Wisselkoers is a de-word.
administration-01.compare: English has the same order: "What is the current exchange rate?"

mistake.why: After de the adjective takes -e.

shopping-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (betaal) second (verb-second order).
shopping-11.forms: Betalen is regular: ik betaal, participle betaald. Mijn stays the same before de-words.
shopping-11.compare: English also says "with" (met) for the means of payment.

mistake.why: Use met for the means of payment.

weather-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-01.forms: After zijn an adjective takes no -e. Het is a dummy subject for weather.
weather-01.compare: English also uses a dummy subject: "It is very foggy".

mistake.why: An adjective after zijn takes no -e.

food-01.meaning: Saying you had already baked the bread.
food-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gebakken) goes to the end.
food-01.forms: Had plus participle is the past perfect: something done before another moment in the past. Bakken: gebakken. Brood is a het-word.
food-01.compare: English also says "I had already baked", with the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.wrong: Ik had het brood gebakken al.
mistake.right: Ik had het brood al gebakken.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

work-01.meaning: Saying you are checking the stock.
work-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (controleer) second (verb-second order).
work-01.forms: Controleren: ik controleer; the participle is gecontroleerd. Voorraad is a de-word.
work-01.compare: English says "I am checking" (progressive); Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: Dutch uses the simple present here.

health-01.meaning: Saying that resting is good for you.
health-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Rusten) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
health-01.forms: The verb is singular because the subject is one activity. No -e on goed after is.
health-01.compare: English uses the -ing form (Resting); Dutch uses the infinitive.

mistake.why: Use the infinitive as the subject.

conversation-12.meaning: Asking for someone's opinion on something.
conversation-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (uw mening) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-12.forms: Uw is the polite your (with u). Hierover is hier plus over: about this.
conversation-12.compare: English says "about this" as two words; Dutch joins hier and over.

mistake.wrong: Wat is uw mening over hier?
mistake.why: Hier and over join into hierover.

conversation-13.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (ging) comes second and the subject (zij) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-13.forms: The simple past of gaan is ging (irregular). Waar ... heen asks where to.
conversation-13.compare: English needs "did" in the question; Dutch just uses ging.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

work-02.meaning: Saying you will prepare a report.
work-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (opstellen) goes to the end.
work-02.forms: Zullen: ik zal. Opstellen is a separable verb but stays whole after a modal. Rapport is a het-word.
work-02.compare: English says "I will prepare a report"; Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

home-11.meaning: Saying they were looking for a flat.
home-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (waren) second (verb-second order).
home-11.forms: The past of zijn: ik was, wij waren, ze waren. Op zoek zijn naar means to look for.
home-11.compare: English uses a progressive ("were looking for"); Dutch uses zijn op zoek naar.

mistake.right: Ze waren op zoek naar een flat.
mistake.why: To look for something is op zoek zijn naar in Dutch, not a plain verb.

work-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De vergadering) comes first and the finite verb (eindigde) second (verb-second order).
work-03.forms: Regular past tense: stem plus -de (eindigen becomes eindigde); the plural ends in -den.
work-03.compare: English "The meeting ended" works the same way.

mistake.why: A singular subject takes -de.

conversation-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gepraat) goes to the end.
conversation-14.forms: Praten: gepraat. Dutch often uses the perfect for a finished event where English uses the simple past.
conversation-14.compare: English says "We talked" (simple past); Dutch says "We have talked".

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

work-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (houd) second (verb-second order).
work-04.forms: Houden: ik houd or ik hou, both are correct. U is the polite you.
work-04.compare: English says "keep you informed"; Dutch says op de hoogte houden.

mistake.right: Ik houd u op de hoogte.
mistake.why: Use the fixed phrase op de hoogte houden.

conversation-15.meaning: Telling the time: half past five.
conversation-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-15.forms: Half zes means half an hour before six, which is 5:30.
conversation-15.compare: English says "half past five"; Dutch counts towards the next hour.

mistake.wrong: Het is half vijf (when you mean 5:30).
mistake.why: Half zes is 5:30; half vijf is 4:30.

weather-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (hou) second (verb-second order).
weather-02.forms: Houden van: both ik hou and ik houd are correct. Zonnige takes -e before the plural dagen.
weather-02.compare: English has no preposition ("love sunny days"); Dutch needs van.

mistake.why: Houden van means to like or love: the preposition van is required.

work-05.meaning: Saying he is done reading the report.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het lezen van het rapport

work-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
work-05.forms: Klaar zijn met means to be finished with. Het lezen is an infinitive used as a noun.
work-05.compare: English says "He has finished reading"; Dutch uses is klaar met.

mistake.wrong: Hij is klaar lezen het rapport.
mistake.right: Hij is klaar met het lezen van het rapport.
mistake.why: To be finished with is klaar zijn met in Dutch.

conversation-16.meaning: Asking if someone will need help.
conversation-16.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Zul), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (hebben) goes to the end.
conversation-16.forms: Zullen with je: the -t drops (zult becomes zul). Hulp nodig hebben means to need help.
conversation-16.compare: English "Will you need help?" has the same inversion.

mistake.why: Start a yes/no question with the finite verb.

conversation-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te blijven) closes the sentence.
conversation-17.forms: Zin hebben om te means to feel like doing something. After te the verb is an infinitive.
conversation-17.compare: English uses an -ing form ("feel like staying"); Dutch uses om te plus infinitive.

mistake.right: We hebben zin om te blijven.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

shopping-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (kocht) second (verb-second order).
shopping-12.forms: Kopen has an irregular past: kocht, plural kochten. Souvenir is a het-word.
shopping-12.compare: English "He bought" is also an irregular past.

mistake.why: The past of kopen is kocht.

weather-03.meaning: Saying you will check the weather.
weather-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (controleren) goes to the end.
weather-03.forms: Zullen: wij zullen. Weer is a het-word.
weather-03.compare: English "We will check the weather" keeps check next to will; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-18.meaning: Saying you have forgotten someone's name.
conversation-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (vergeten) goes to the end.
conversation-18.forms: Vergeten usually takes zijn in the perfect. Je means your before a noun.
conversation-18.compare: English says "I have forgotten"; Dutch usually says "I am forgotten (your name)".

mistake.why: The usual perfect of vergeten is ben vergeten.

transport-11.meaning: Asking if a place can be reached on foot.
transport-11.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it.
transport-11.forms: Te plus infinitive here means can be done: te lopen.
transport-11.compare: English "Can you walk there?" is built differently.

mistake.why: Use te before the infinitive in this phrase.

food-02.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it.
food-02.forms: Mogen: ik mag. Wat before a noun means some.
food-02.compare: English says "May I have some water?"; Dutch drops have.

mistake.why: Start with mag to ask permission.

work-06.meaning: Promising to get back to someone about something.
work-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kom) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (terug) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
work-06.forms: Terugkomen op splits in a main clause: ik kom ... terug. Er plus op becomes erop.
work-06.compare: English "I will get back to it" uses a different verb; Dutch uses terugkomen op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

food-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedronken) goes to the end.
food-03.forms: Drinken: gedronken. Dutch often uses the perfect where English uses the simple past.
food-03.compare: English says "We drank coffee"; Dutch says "We have drunk coffee".

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

transport-12.meaning: Saying someone left an hour ago.
transport-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (vertrokken) goes to the end.
transport-12.forms: Vertrekken uses zijn (it is a verb of movement): is vertrokken. Geleden follows the time and means ago.
transport-12.compare: English says "He left an hour ago" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.wrong: Hij heeft een uur geleden vertrokken.
mistake.right: Hij is een uur geleden vertrokken.
mistake.why: Verbs of leaving use zijn.

home-12.meaning: Saying you would rather stay at home.
home-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (blijf) second (verb-second order).
home-12.forms: Liever is the comparative of graag.
home-12.compare: English says "would rather"; Dutch just uses liever.

mistake.why: The comparative of graag is liever.

work-07.order: In the past tense the verb is second and the particle schoon goes to the end.
work-07.forms: Schoonmaken splits: maakte ... schoon. Bureau is a het-word.
work-07.compare: English "She cleaned the desk" has no separate particle.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

conversation-19.meaning: Saying something sounded a little strange.
conversation-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (klonk) second (verb-second order).
conversation-19.forms: Klinken has an irregular past: klonk. After klinken the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-19.compare: English "It sounded somewhat strange" is the same.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

health-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
health-02.compare: English "I need a doctor" is one verb; Dutch splits it around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

conversation-20.meaning: Asking someone to say if they need anything.
conversation-20.order: The first part is an imperative. After als the clause is subordinate, so the finite verb hebt goes to the very end.
conversation-20.forms: Laat het me weten means let me know. Hebt is the je-form of hebben when je comes before the verb.
conversation-20.compare: English keeps "need" next to "you"; Dutch moves hebt to the end.

mistake.wrong: Laat het me weten als je hebt iets nodig.
mistake.right: Laat het me weten als je iets nodig hebt.
mistake.why: After als the finite verb goes to the end.

leisure-01.meaning: Saying they have seen the film.
leisure-01.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gezien) goes to the end.
leisure-01.forms: Zien has an irregular participle: gezien.
leisure-01.compare: English "They have seen the film" is the same idea.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

work-08.meaning: Saying you are confirming the details.
work-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (bevestig) second (verb-second order).
work-08.forms: Bevestigen: ik bevestig; the participle is bevestigd (no ge-).
work-08.compare: English says "I am confirming"; Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: With ik the verb loses -en.

work-09.meaning: Saying she is busy writing an email.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met het schrijven van een e-mail

work-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
work-09.forms: Bezig zijn met means to be busy with. Het schrijven is an infinitive used as a noun.
work-09.compare: English says "busy writing"; Dutch says bezig met het schrijven.

mistake.wrong: Ze is bezig schrijven een e-mail.
mistake.right: Ze is druk bezig met het schrijven van een e-mail.
mistake.why: To be busy with is bezig zijn met in Dutch.

conversation-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). Eens goes to the end of the clause.
conversation-21.forms: Het eens zijn met means to agree with. Daarmee is da plus met: with that.
conversation-21.compare: English says "I agree with that"; Dutch says ik ben het ermee eens (literally "I am it with-that agreed").

mistake.why: Include het and put eens last.

leisure-02.meaning: Saying what you used to do.
leisure-02.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ging) second (verb-second order).
leisure-02.forms: Gaan has an irregular past: ging.
leisure-02.compare: English says "I used to go"; Dutch uses the simple past with vroeger.

mistake.wrong: Ik gaan vroeger naar de bioscoop.
mistake.right: Ik ging vroeger naar de bioscoop.
mistake.why: Gaan is irregular: the past is ging (singular) and gingen (plural).

transport-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (vertrokken) second (verb-second order).
transport-13.forms: Vertrekken has an irregular past: vertrok (singular), vertrokken (plural).
transport-13.compare: English "They left early." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of vertrekken is irregular.

conversation-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dat) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-22.forms: Idee is a het-word, so after een the adjective takes no -e: een geweldig idee.
conversation-22.compare: English "That is a great idea!" has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: Het-word after een: no -e.

conversation-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-23.forms: Waard zijn means to be worth. Het proberen is an infinitive used as a noun.
conversation-23.compare: English says "worth trying"; Dutch says het proberen waard.

mistake.why: Waard goes to the end of this expression: het proberen waard.

work-10.meaning: Asking to work together on this.
work-10.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (samenwerken) goes to the end.
work-10.forms: Hieraan is hier plus aan: on this.
work-10.compare: English says "work together on this"; the order is similar.

mistake.why: Put hieraan before the infinitive.

leisure-03.meaning: Saying they are practising their drawing skills.
leisure-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (oefenen) second (verb-second order).
leisure-03.forms: Oefenen: ze oefenen (plural). Hun means their before a noun.
leisure-03.compare: English "They are practising" is a progressive; Dutch uses the simple present.

mistake.why: The possessive for they is hun, placed before the noun.

conversation-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (belde) second (verb-second order).
conversation-24.forms: Bellen is regular: belde. Jou is the stressed object form of je.
conversation-24.compare: English "She called you." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Use the object form jou (or je).

conversation-25.meaning: Saying you have met new people.
conversation-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (ontmoet) goes to the end.
conversation-25.forms: Ontmoeten has no ge- in the participle (ont- is an inseparable prefix). Nieuwe takes -e before the plural.
conversation-25.compare: English says "I met" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: Verbs that start with ont- have no ge-.

weather-04.meaning: Saying it is about to rain.
weather-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (regenen) goes to the end. Gaan plus an infinitive says what is about to happen.
weather-04.forms: Gaan: het gaat. There is no te after gaan.
weather-04.compare: English says "It is going to rain"; Dutch is the same idea.

mistake.why: After gaan the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

home-13.meaning: Saying he is responsible for tidying up.
home-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-13.forms: Verantwoordelijk zijn voor means to be responsible for.
home-13.compare: English "responsible for tidying up" uses -ing; Dutch uses voor het opruimen (an infinitive used as a noun).

mistake.wrong: Hij is verantwoordelijk om het opruimen.
mistake.right: Hij is verantwoordelijk voor het opruimen.
mistake.why: Use voor after verantwoordelijk.

food-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (dronk) second (verb-second order).
food-04.forms: Drinken has an irregular past: dronk, plural dronken.
food-04.compare: English "I drank a lemonade" is an irregular past too; Dutch drinken becomes dronk (singular) and dronken (plural).

mistake.why: The past of drinken is dronk.

conversation-26.meaning: Saying that thinking of someone makes you smile.
conversation-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Aan jou denken) comes first and the finite verb (doet) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (glimlachen) goes to the end.
conversation-26.forms: Doen plus an infinitive means to make someone do something. There is no te.
conversation-26.compare: English says "makes me smile"; Dutch says doet me glimlachen.

mistake.wrong: Aan jou denken doet me te glimlachen.
mistake.right: Aan jou denken doet me glimlachen.
mistake.why: After doen the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

home-14.meaning: Saying you need to charge your phone.
home-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (moet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (opladen) goes to the end.
home-14.forms: Moeten: ik moet. Opladen stays whole after a modal.
home-14.compare: English says "I need to charge my phone"; Dutch puts opladen last.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

school-11.meaning: Telling someone to keep trying until they understand.
school-11.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Blijf) and leaves out the subject. After totdat the clause is subordinate, so its finite verb (snapt) moves to the very end.
school-11.forms: Blijven plus an infinitive means to keep on doing. Snappen: je snapt.
school-11.compare: English says "until you get it"; Dutch moves snapt to the end.

mistake.wrong: Blijf proberen totdat je snapt het.
mistake.right: Blijf proberen totdat je het snapt.
mistake.why: After totdat the verb goes to the end.

work-11.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wanneer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de deadline) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
work-11.compare: English "When is the deadline?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

work-12.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive goes to the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (plannen) goes to the end.
work-12.compare: English "Let's schedule a follow-up" uses let's plus a bare verb; Dutch uses laten we plus an infinitive at the end.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

transport-14.meaning: Asking if it is a long walk.
transport-14.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (lopen) goes to the end.
transport-14.forms: Ver lopen asks about distance on foot.
transport-14.compare: English "Is it a long walk?" uses a noun (walk); Dutch uses the infinitive lopen after ver: is het ver lopen?

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

transport-15.meaning: Saying it is opposite the park.
transport-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
transport-15.compare: English "It is opposite the park." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: Park is a het-word, so the article is het.

work-13.meaning: Saying you are used to working long hours.
work-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the te phrase (te werken) closes the sentence.
work-13.forms: Gewend zijn te. Lange takes -e before plural.
work-13.compare: English "I am used to working long hours." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ik ben gewend werken lange uren.
mistake.right: Ik ben gewend lange uren te werken.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive.

school-12.meaning: Telling someone to explain it to you.
school-12.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Leg) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (uit) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
school-12.compare: English "Explain it to me" is one verb; Dutch splits uitleggen: leg het me uit, with uit at the end.

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle last.

transport-16.meaning: Asking where someone will be staying.
transport-16.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zult) comes second and the subject (u) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verblijven) goes to the end.
transport-16.compare: English "Where will you be staying?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-27.meaning: Saying you had already heard a story before.
conversation-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gehoord) goes to the end.
conversation-27.forms: Had plus participle is the past perfect. Horen: gehoord. Verhaal is a het-word, so dat.
conversation-27.compare: English "I had heard that story before" keeps the participle next to had; Dutch puts it last.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gehoord dat verhaal al eens.
mistake.right: Ik had dat verhaal al eens gehoord.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-28.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (moet) comes second and the subject (ik) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (doen) goes to the end.
conversation-28.compare: English "What should I do?" has the same order.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dat) comes first and the finite verb (klinkt) second (verb-second order).
conversation-29.forms: Klinken: dat klinkt. No -e after klinken.
conversation-29.compare: English "That sounds great!" has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

food-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (heb) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegeten) goes to the end.
food-05.forms: Perfect: heb je gegeten. Eten: gegeten.
food-05.compare: English says "Where did you eat?" (simple past); Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-30.meaning: Saying you had already made a choice.
conversation-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gemaakt) goes to the end.
conversation-30.forms: Hadden plus participle is the past perfect (plural). Een keuze maken means to make a choice.
conversation-30.compare: English "We had already made a choice" keeps the participle next to had.

mistake.wrong: We hadden gemaakt al een keuze.
mistake.right: We hadden al een keuze gemaakt.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

shopping-13.order: This is a noun phrase with no verb: a number, the unit dozijn (which stays singular after a number) and the thing counted.
shopping-13.forms: After a number, dozijn stays singular. Ei is a het-word with an irregular plural: eieren.
shopping-13.compare: English says "two dozen eggs" with dozen in the plural; Dutch keeps dozijn singular after a number: twee dozijn eieren.

mistake.why: After a number, dozijn stays singular.

work-14.meaning: Suggesting that you set a new deadline.
work-14.order: Laten we plus an infinitive makes a suggestion; the infinitive goes to the end.
work-14.compare: English says "Let's set a new deadline"; Dutch ends with the infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Laten we stellen een nieuwe deadline.
mistake.right: Laten we een nieuwe deadline stellen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

administration-02.meaning: Asking for something to be sent to you.
administration-02.order: Laat plus object plus infinitive means have it done. The infinitive goes to the end.
administration-02.forms: Laten here means to have something done. Opsturen stays whole.
administration-02.compare: English says "Have it sent to me"; Dutch uses the infinitive opsturen.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

food-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te eten) closes the sentence.
food-06.forms: Zin hebben om te means to feel like.
food-06.compare: English "I feel like eating." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Ik heb zin om te eten.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

work-15.meaning: Saying you talked about the project.
work-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hebben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gesproken) goes to the end.
work-15.forms: Spreken: gesproken. Spreken over means to talk about.
work-15.compare: English says "We talked about"; Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.wrong: We hebben gesproken over het project.
mistake.right: We hebben over het project gesproken.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

transport-17.meaning: Asking if someone knows an area.
transport-17.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kent), and the subject (u) follows it.
transport-17.forms: Kennen: u kent. Use kennen for people and places; weten for facts.
transport-17.compare: English says "Do you know this neighbourhood?"; Dutch just inverts.

mistake.why: Start with the finite verb to ask the question.

conversation-31.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-31.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-31.compare: English "I am so proud." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-32.meaning: Asking what someone is doing right now.
conversation-32.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (ben) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (doen) goes to the end.
conversation-32.forms: Zijn aan het plus infinitive shows an action in progress.
conversation-32.compare: English "What are you doing?" uses the -ing form.

mistake.wrong: Wat je bent aan het doen?
mistake.right: Wat ben je aan het doen?
mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

leisure-04.meaning: Saying you are looking forward to the holiday.
leisure-04.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (kijken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (uit) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
leisure-04.forms: Uitkijken naar splits: we kijken ... uit naar.
leisure-04.compare: English "We are looking forward to" is a phrasal verb; Dutch splits its separable verb.

mistake.right: We kijken uit naar de vakantie.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-15.meaning: Saying you had already turned off the lights.
home-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (uitgedaan) goes to the end.
home-15.forms: Uitdoen: uitgedaan (ge- goes between uit and gedaan).
home-15.compare: English "turned off" has a particle after the object; Dutch keeps it inside the participle.

mistake.wrong: Ik had de lichten al gedaan uit.
mistake.right: Ik had de lichten al uitgedaan.
mistake.why: The separable participle is one word: uitgedaan.

transport-18.meaning: Telling someone to walk down a street.
transport-18.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Loop) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (af) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-18.forms: Aflopen splits in an imperative: loop ... af.
transport-18.compare: English "Walk down this street" has no particle.

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle goes last.

shopping-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order).
shopping-14.forms: Willen: ik wil. The verb hebben is left out.
shopping-14.compare: English "I would like this" uses would; Dutch uses the present.

mistake.why: The finite verb stays second.

transport-19.meaning: Asking if there is free wifi.
transport-19.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (gratis wifi) follows it.
transport-19.forms: Er is introduces something that exists.
transport-19.compare: English "Is there free Wi-Fi?" also starts with the verb and uses there; Dutch uses er in the same place.

mistake.why: Start with the verb to ask the question.

food-07.meaning: Saying you tried a new dish.
food-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (probeerde) second (verb-second order).
food-07.forms: Regular past: proberen becomes probeerde. Gerecht is a het-word, so nieuw has no -e after een.
food-07.compare: English "I tried a new dish." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: A het-word after een takes no -e.

food-08.meaning: Politely asking to see the menu.
food-08.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Mag), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zien) goes to the end.
food-08.forms: Mogen: ik mag. Menukaart is a de-word.
food-08.compare: English "May I see the menu?" has the same order.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

weather-05.meaning: Saying it is very cold here.
weather-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-05.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
weather-05.compare: English "It is very cold here." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

work-16.meaning: Saying you had finished the project early.
work-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (afgerond) goes to the end.
work-16.compare: English "We had finished the project early" keeps the participle next to had.

mistake.wrong: We hadden afgerond het project vroeg.
mistake.right: We hadden het project vroeg afgerond.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-33.meaning: A polite way to say thank you very much.
conversation-33.order: A fixed polite expression with no verb: an adverb (hartelijk) in front of the noun dank.
conversation-33.forms: Hartelijk is an adverb here and does not change.
conversation-33.compare: English says "Thank you very much"; Dutch uses the fixed phrase hartelijk dank, with no verb.

mistake.why: The adverb hartelijk does not take -e here.

transport-20.meaning: Asking where the train station is.
transport-20.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het treinstation) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-20.compare: English "Where is the train station?" is the same.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-09.meaning: Suggesting to go and have a cup of coffee.
food-09.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive goes to the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (gaan) goes to the end; the infinitive (drinken) goes to the end.
food-09.forms: Gaan plus infinitive means go and do.
food-09.compare: English "Let's go and have a cup of coffee" uses let's plus go and have; Dutch puts both infinitives at the end: laten we ... gaan drinken.

mistake.wrong: Laten we gaan drinken een kop koffie.
mistake.right: Laten we een kop koffie gaan drinken.
mistake.why: The infinitives go to the end.

conversation-34.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (leek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-34.forms: Lijken: leek (irregular past). No -e after lijken.
conversation-34.compare: English "He seemed very happy." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

weather-06.order: Er takes the first position, so the finite verb (was) is second and the real subject comes after it.
weather-06.compare: English "There was a thunderstorm" is the same.

mistake.why: The verb agrees with the singular noun: was.

food-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (betaald) goes to the end.
food-10.forms: Betalen: betaald. English uses the simple past here.
food-10.compare: English says "I paid the bill"; Dutch uses the perfect.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

leisure-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe vaak) takes the first position, so the finite verb (train) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
leisure-05.forms: Trainen: je traint, but the -t drops when je follows: train je.
leisure-05.compare: English "How often do you train?" needs do; Dutch just inverts.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject; -t drops after je.

work-17.meaning: Saying you will discuss it then.
work-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (bespreken) goes to the end.
work-17.compare: English "We will discuss it then" keeps discuss next to will.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

leisure-06.meaning: Suggesting to go for a run.
leisure-06.order: Laten we is the fixed way to make a suggestion: the verb comes first, then we, and the infinitive goes to the end. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (gaan) goes to the end; the infinitive (hardlopen) goes to the end.
leisure-06.forms: Gaan plus infinitive means go and do.
leisure-06.compare: English "Let's go running" uses an -ing form; Dutch uses two infinitives: laten we gaan hardlopen.

mistake.why: Gaan comes before the other infinitive.

shopping-15.meaning: Saying he is busy closing the shop.
shopping-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the te phrase (te sluiten) closes the sentence.
shopping-15.compare: English "He is busy closing the shop" is similar.

mistake.wrong: Hij is bezig sluiten de winkel.
mistake.right: Hij is bezig de winkel te sluiten.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive at the end.

work-18.meaning: Saying you are thinking about opening a shop.
work-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (denken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om een winkel te openen) closes the sentence.
work-18.forms: Er plus over becomes erover. After te comes an infinitive.
work-18.compare: English "We are thinking about opening a shop" uses -ing.

mistake.wrong: We denken erover om een winkel openen.
mistake.right: We denken erover om een winkel te openen.
mistake.why: After om the infinitive needs te.

shopping-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) goes to the end.
shopping-16.compare: English "I bought this yesterday" is the simple past.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-35.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (afspreken) goes to the end.
conversation-35.forms: Days have no article here. Afspreken stays whole after a modal.
conversation-35.compare: English "Can we meet on Tuesday?" is the same order.

mistake.why: Start with the finite verb.

health-03.meaning: Saying you felt a little tired.
health-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (voelde) second (verb-second order).
health-03.compare: English "I felt a little tired" has no reflexive pronoun; Dutch zich voelen needs one: ik voelde me.

mistake.right: Ik voelde me een beetje moe.
mistake.why: Zich voelen needs the reflexive pronoun.

administration-03.meaning: Saying you had already written the letter.
administration-03.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (geschreven) goes to the end.
administration-03.compare: English "I had already written the letter." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (geschreven) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ik had geschreven de brief al.
mistake.right: Ik had de brief al geschreven.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-36.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kan), and the subject (ik) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (krijgen) goes to the end.
conversation-36.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Nummer is a het-word.
conversation-36.compare: English "Can I have your number?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: Start with the finite verb.

transport-21.meaning: Promising to show someone the way.
transport-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (wijzen) goes to the end.
transport-21.forms: Zullen: ik zal. De weg wijzen means to show the way.
transport-21.compare: English "I will show you the way." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (wijzen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik zal wijzen je de weg.
mistake.right: Ik zal je de weg wijzen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-37.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (terugbellen) goes to the end.
conversation-37.forms: In a main clause terugbellen would split: hij belt terug.
conversation-37.compare: English "He will call back" has back after the verb; Dutch keeps terugbellen as one word after zal.

mistake.why: After a modal the separable verb stays whole.

transport-22.meaning: Politely asking someone to show you the way.
transport-22.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunt), and the subject (u) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (wijzen) goes to the end.
transport-22.forms: Kunnen with u: u kunt (u kan also occurs). Mij is the object form.
transport-22.compare: English "Can you show me the way?" has the same order.

mistake.wrong: Kunt u wijzen mij de weg?
mistake.right: Kunt u mij de weg wijzen?
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

weather-07.meaning: Asking if it is cold outside.
weather-07.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it.
weather-07.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
weather-07.compare: English "Is it cold outside?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

conversation-38.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Kunnen), and the subject (we) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verzetten) goes to the end.
conversation-38.compare: English "Can we reschedule this?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-39.meaning: Saying he hid something from us.
conversation-39.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verborgen) goes to the end.
conversation-39.compare: English "He hid it from us." uses the simple past; Dutch often uses the perfect (auxiliary plus participle) for a finished event, with the participle (verborgen) at the end.

mistake.wrong: Hij heeft verborgen het voor ons.
mistake.right: Hij heeft het voor ons verborgen.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

shopping-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (droeg) second (verb-second order).
shopping-17.compare: English "She wore a scarf" is the same simple past; the Dutch verb dragen has an irregular past: droeg.

mistake.why: The past of dragen is droeg.

conversation-40.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (nam) second (verb-second order).
conversation-40.forms: Nemen: nam (irregular). Een beslissing nemen means to decide.
conversation-40.compare: English "I made a decision" uses make; Dutch uses nemen.

mistake.why: Use nemen with beslissing.

home-16.meaning: Saying your phone battery is dead.
home-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Mijn telefoon) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-16.forms: Leeg means empty; Dutch uses it for a dead battery.
home-16.compare: English says "My phone is dead"; Dutch says mijn telefoon is leeg (empty).

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

health-04.meaning: Saying they will sit and wait until the doctor calls.
health-04.order: The main clause has the verb second. After tot the clause is subordinate, so the verb goes to the end.
health-04.forms: Gaan zitten means to sit down.
health-04.compare: English "until the doctor calls them" keeps calls near doctor.

mistake.why: After tot the verb goes to the end.

conversation-41.meaning: Saying she is happy about the chance.
conversation-41.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-41.forms: Blij zijn met means to be happy about.
conversation-41.compare: English "happy about" uses about; Dutch uses met.

mistake.wrong: Ze blij is met de kans.
mistake.right: Ze is blij met de kans.
mistake.why: The finite verb stays second: ze is blij. Blij zijn met means to be happy about something.

food-11.meaning: Asking where the bag of food is.
food-11.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de zak) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
food-11.forms: Met links a container to its contents.
food-11.compare: English "Where is the bag of food?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.wrong: Waar de zak met eten is?
mistake.right: Waar is de zak met eten?
mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-42.meaning: Saying it did not work the first time.
conversation-42.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (werkte) second (verb-second order).
conversation-42.compare: English "It did not work" needs "did"; Dutch has no helper verb: het werkte ... niet.

mistake.wrong: Het niet werkte de eerste keer.
mistake.right: Het werkte de eerste keer niet.
mistake.why: Niet comes after the time phrase.

conversation-43.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-43.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
conversation-43.compare: English "It is very blurry" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to wazig after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

shopping-18.meaning: Asking if someone bought it for you.
shopping-18.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heb), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) goes to the end.
shopping-18.forms: Heb je: the -t drops after je.
shopping-18.compare: English "Did you buy it for me?" needs "did" to form the question; Dutch just starts with the finite verb (Heb).

mistake.wrong: Je hebt het voor me gekocht?
mistake.right: Heb je het voor me gekocht?
mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the auxiliary, before the subject.

school-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
school-13.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
school-13.compare: English "This is very easy" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to gemakkelijk after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

transport-23.meaning: Saying they leave for a holiday on Friday.
transport-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (vertrekken) second (verb-second order).
transport-23.forms: Op vakantie vertrekken means to leave for a holiday.
transport-23.compare: English "They are leaving on holiday on Friday" uses a progressive.

mistake.why: A day used as a time phrase takes no op: vrijdag, not op vrijdag.

school-14.meaning: Telling someone to read it aloud to you.
school-14.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Lees) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (voor) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
school-14.forms: Voorlezen splits in an imperative: lees ... voor.
school-14.compare: English "Read it aloud to me." is also a command with no subject; Dutch starts with the verb (Lees).

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle goes last.

transport-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
transport-24.forms: Nodig hebben. Kaart is a de-word.
transport-24.compare: English "I need a map" is one verb; Dutch splits ik heb ... nodig around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

leisure-07.meaning: Saying you are here to play.
leisure-07.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (zijn) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te spelen) closes the sentence.
leisure-07.forms: Om te plus infinitive shows purpose.
leisure-07.compare: English "We are here to play." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Wij zijn hier om te spelen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

health-05.meaning: Saying you wash your hands before every meal.
health-05.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (was) second (verb-second order).
health-05.compare: English "I wash my hands before every meal." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Ik was handen mijn voor elke maaltijd.
mistake.right: Ik was mijn handen voor elke maaltijd.
mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

transport-25.meaning: Saying you are ready to go.
transport-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te gaan) closes the sentence.
transport-25.compare: English "I am ready to go" uses to; Dutch needs om te: klaar om te gaan.
