mistake.right: Ik ben klaar om te gaan.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

work-19.meaning: Saying he sometimes arrives late because of traffic.
work-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (komt) second (verb-second order).
work-19.forms: Te laat komen means to arrive late.
work-19.compare: English "He sometimes arrives late because of traffic." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Hij komt soms te laat door de verkeer.
mistake.right: Hij komt soms te laat door het verkeer.
mistake.why: Verkeer is a het-word, so het.

home-17.meaning: Saying they wanted to move to a bigger house.
home-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (wilden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (verhuizen) goes to the end.
home-17.forms: Willen: ze wilden (past plural). Groter huis: no -e after een with a het-word.
home-17.compare: English "They wanted to move to a bigger house".

mistake.wrong: Ze wilden naar een grotere huis verhuizen.
mistake.right: Ze wilden naar een groter huis verhuizen.
mistake.why: Huis is a het-word: after een the adjective takes no -e.

transport-26.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het toilet) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-26.compare: English "Where is the toilet?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

health-06.meaning: Saying she will become a great doctor one day.
health-06.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (wordt) second (verb-second order).
health-06.forms: Worden: ze wordt. Geweldige takes -e before the de-word dokter.
health-06.compare: English "She will be a great doctor" uses will.

mistake.wrong: Ze wordt op een dag een geweldig dokter.
mistake.right: Ze wordt op een dag een geweldige dokter.
mistake.why: After een, a de-word takes -e.

weather-08.meaning: Saying it was a beautiful sunset.
weather-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (was) second (verb-second order).
weather-08.forms: Zijn: het was. Prachtige takes -e before the de-word zonsondergang.
weather-08.compare: English "It was a beautiful sunset" has the same pattern; the Dutch past of zijn is was (singular) and waren (plural).

mistake.why: After een a de-word takes -e.

work-20.meaning: Saying they used the meeting room for the presentation.
work-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gebruikten) second (verb-second order).
work-20.compare: English "They used the meeting room for the presentation".

mistake.wrong: Ze gebruikte de vergaderruimte voor de presentatie.
mistake.right: Ze gebruikten de vergaderruimte voor de presentatie.
mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den/-ten.

work-21.meaning: Saying you will know the results by Monday.

work-21.forms: Weten: ik weet. Uiterlijk means at the latest.

mistake.wrong: Ik weet de resultaten uiterlijk bij maandag.

mistake.why: No preposition is needed before the day after uiterlijk.

leisure-08.meaning: Saying you will dance with someone at the wedding.
leisure-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (dans) second (verb-second order).
leisure-08.forms: Dansen met means to dance with. The present tense can express a plan, so ik dans can mean I will dance.
leisure-08.compare: English "I will dance with you at the wedding" uses will; Dutch uses the present tense for a plan: ik dans met je.

mistake.wrong: Ik dans je met op de bruiloft.
mistake.right: Ik dans met je op de bruiloft.
mistake.why: The preposition comes before its pronoun: met je.

conversation-44.meaning: Saying you want to send it to someone.
conversation-44.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (sturen) goes to the end.
conversation-44.compare: English "I want to send it to you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (sturen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-45.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (helpen) goes to the end.
conversation-45.compare: English "We will help you" uses will; Dutch uses zullen with the infinitive helpen at the end.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

conversation-46.meaning: Saying they are on their way.
conversation-46.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (komen) second (verb-second order).
conversation-46.forms: Eraan komen means to be on the way.
conversation-46.compare: English "They are coming" is a progressive; Dutch zij komen eraan also means they are on their way.

mistake.why: Zij komen aan means they arrive; to say they are on their way you need eraan.

conversation-47.meaning: Saying you are only a guest.
conversation-47.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-47.forms: Maar here means only. Zijn: ik ben.
conversation-47.compare: English "I am only a guest" uses only; Dutch uses maar.

mistake.why: The article comes before the noun.

leisure-09.meaning: Saying you will come to someone's party.
leisure-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kom) second (verb-second order).
leisure-09.forms: Komen naar a place or event. Feestje is a het-word.
leisure-09.compare: English "I will come to your party" uses will; Dutch uses the present.

mistake.why: Use naar for the event you go to.

home-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
home-18.forms: After zijn the adjective takes no -e.
home-18.compare: English "It is very dirty" has the same pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

conversation-48.meaning: Telling someone to give it to you.
conversation-48.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Geef) and leaves out the subject.
conversation-48.compare: English "Give it to me" uses to; Dutch puts the person straight after the object: geef het me.

mistake.why: The imperative uses the stem, not the infinitive.

leisure-10.meaning: Saying you danced with your wife at the reception.
leisure-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (danste) second (verb-second order).
leisure-10.forms: Dansen: danste (regular). Vrouw is a de-word.
leisure-10.compare: English "I danced with my wife at the reception." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.wrong: Ik dansde met mijn vrouw op de receptie.
mistake.right: Ik danste met mijn vrouw op de receptie.
mistake.why: After a stem ending in s, the past takes -te, not -de.

home-19.meaning: Saying you used to stay up late.
home-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (bleven) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-19.forms: Opblijven splits: bleven ... op. Blijven: bleef, bleven.
home-19.compare: English "We used to stay up late" keeps up after the verb; Dutch splits opblijven: wij bleven ... op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

weather-09.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (wordt) second (verb-second order).
weather-09.forms: Worden plus adjective describes a change; no -e.
weather-09.compare: English "It is getting cold" uses getting; Dutch uses worden: het wordt koud.

mistake.why: After worden the adjective takes no -e ending.

home-20.meaning: Saying you lived in the city.
home-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (woonden) second (verb-second order).
home-20.compare: English "We lived in the city." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

leisure-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gekocht) goes to the end.
leisure-11.compare: English "She bought the tickets" uses the simple past.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-49.meaning: Saying it is difficult to help.
conversation-49.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te helpen) closes the sentence.
conversation-49.forms: Het is plus adjective plus om te plus infinitive.
conversation-49.compare: English "It is difficult to help." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Het is moeilijk om te helpen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive.

conversation-50.meaning: Saying you are thinking about the name.
conversation-50.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (denk) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (na) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
conversation-50.forms: Nadenken splits: ik denk na. Over introduces the topic.
conversation-50.compare: English "I am thinking about the name" has no particle; Dutch splits nadenken: ik denk na over de naam.

mistake.right: Ik denk na over de naam.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause.

weather-10.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (keken) second (verb-second order).
weather-10.compare: English "We watched the sunset." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Kijken needs naar before what you look at.

administration-04.meaning: Asking if someone will send it to you.
administration-04.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Stuur), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
administration-04.forms: Opsturen splits: stuur je ... op. The -t drops after je.
administration-04.compare: English "Will you send it to me?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: Start with the verb to ask.

weather-11.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De maan) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
weather-11.compare: English "The moon is bright" has the same pattern; Dutch adds no ending to helder after is.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

work-22.meaning: Saying she received an award for her work.
work-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (ontving) second (verb-second order).
work-22.compare: English "She received an award for her work." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of ontvangen is ontving.

food-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Hoe) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het ontbijt) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
food-12.compare: English "How is the breakfast?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-51.meaning: Saying you had already seen the news.
conversation-51.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gezien) goes to the end.
conversation-51.forms: Zien: gezien. Nieuws is a het-word.
conversation-51.compare: English "I had already seen the news." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (gezien) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gezien het nieuws al.
mistake.right: Ik had het nieuws al gezien.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

school-15.meaning: Saying you cannot explain it to someone.
school-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (uitleggen) goes to the end.
school-15.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Het je: the thing first, then the person.
school-15.compare: English "I cannot explain it to you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (uitleggen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan niet het je uitleggen.
mistake.right: Ik kan het je niet uitleggen.
mistake.why: Niet comes after the pronouns, before the infinitive.

conversation-52.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-52.forms: Fout is a de-word; mijn does not change.
conversation-52.compare: English "It is my fault" is the same pattern; Dutch fout is a de-word, and mijn stays the same.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

transport-27.meaning: Saying you were standing waiting at the bus stop.
transport-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (stond) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (te wachten) goes to the end.
transport-27.forms: Staan te plus infinitive describes an ongoing action.
transport-27.compare: English "I was waiting"; Dutch says stond te wachten.

mistake.wrong: Ik stond wachten bij de bushalte.
mistake.right: Ik stond te wachten bij de bushalte.
mistake.why: Add te before the infinitive.

food-13.meaning: Saying she did not drink her coffee.
food-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedronken) goes to the end.
food-13.compare: English "She did not drink her coffee" uses did not.

mistake.wrong: Ze heeft niet haar koffie gedronken.
mistake.right: Ze heeft haar koffie niet gedronken.
mistake.why: Niet comes after the object, before the participle.

home-21.meaning: Asking if someone is sleeping now.
home-21.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Slaap), and the subject (je) follows it.
home-21.forms: Slapen: je slaapt, but the -t drops after je.
home-21.compare: English "Are you sleeping now?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: Start with the verb; -t drops after je.

shopping-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kocht) second (verb-second order).
shopping-19.forms: Kopen: kocht. Wat before a noun means some.
shopping-19.compare: English "I bought some fruit." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: The past of kopen is kocht.

work-23.meaning: Saying they are talking about the details.
work-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (praten) second (verb-second order).
work-23.compare: English "They are talking about the details" is a progressive; Dutch uses the simple present: ze praten over de details.

mistake.why: Use over before the topic.

transport-28.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het bed) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
transport-28.compare: English "Where is the bed?" has the same order; Dutch bed is a het-word, so het bed.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-53.meaning: Telling someone to give it back to you.
conversation-53.order: An imperative (a command or request) begins with the verb (Geef) and leaves out the subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (terug) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
conversation-53.compare: English "Give it back to us" keeps back after the verb; Dutch puts terug at the very end: geef het ons terug.

mistake.why: The verb comes first; the particle goes last.

transport-29.meaning: Saying you fly with the same airline every time.
transport-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (vliegen) second (verb-second order).
transport-29.forms: Dezelfde goes with de-words (luchtvaartmaatschappij); het-words take hetzelfde.
transport-29.compare: English always says "the same"; Dutch has dezelfde (de-words and plurals) and hetzelfde (het-words).

mistake.why: Luchtvaartmaatschappij is a de-word, so dezelfde.

conversation-54.meaning: Saying you cannot tell someone yet.
conversation-54.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (kan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vertellen) goes to the end.
conversation-54.forms: Kunnen: ik kan. Nog niet means not yet.
conversation-54.compare: English "I cannot tell you yet." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (vertellen) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik kan het je vertellen nog niet.
mistake.right: Ik kan het je nog niet vertellen.
mistake.why: Nog niet comes before the infinitive.

home-22.meaning: Saying they are thinking about moving.
home-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (denken) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te verhuizen) closes the sentence.
home-22.compare: English "They are thinking about moving" uses -ing; Dutch uses erover om te verhuizen.

mistake.right: Ze denken erover om te verhuizen.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive after om.

transport-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
transport-30.compare: English "It is over there"; Dutch daarginds is a single word for a place further away than daar.

mistake.why: Daarginds is written as one word.

conversation-55.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Spreekt), and the subject (u) follows it.
conversation-55.compare: English "Do you speak English?" needs "do" to form the question; Dutch just starts with the finite verb (Spreekt).

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

leisure-12.meaning: Saying they made plans for the weekend.
leisure-12.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (maakten) second (verb-second order).
leisure-12.compare: English "They made plans" is the same simple past; Dutch maken is regular: maakten in the plural.

mistake.wrong: Ze maakte plannen voor het weekend.
mistake.right: Ze maakten plannen voor het weekend.
mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den/-ten.

school-16.meaning: Telling someone they need to listen.
school-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (moet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (luisteren) goes to the end.
school-16.compare: English "You need to listen" uses to; Dutch uses je moet plus a bare infinitive, with no te.

mistake.why: After a modal verb the infinitive follows directly, with no te.

leisure-13.meaning: Saying they were watching the match.
leisure-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (keken) second (verb-second order).
leisure-13.compare: English "They were watching the match" is a past progressive; Dutch uses the simple past keken, followed by naar.

mistake.why: Kijken needs naar before what you look at.

shopping-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).

conversation-57.meaning: Saying they asked us to come early.

transport-31.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (passeerden) second (verb-second order).

mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

leisure-14.meaning: Saying you did not lose the match.
leisure-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (hebt) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verloren) goes to the end.

mistake.wrong: Je hebt niet de wedstrijd verloren.
mistake.right: Je hebt de wedstrijd niet verloren.
mistake.why: Niet comes after the object.

shopping-21.meaning: Saying they paid cash for the furniture.
shopping-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (betaalden) second (verb-second order).
shopping-21.compare: English "They paid cash for the furniture." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.wrong: Ze betaalde contant voor de meubels.
mistake.right: Ze betaalden contant voor de meubels.
mistake.why: A plural subject takes -den.

home-25.meaning: Saying you hear the birds singing every morning.
home-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (hoor) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zingen) goes to the end. After horen you can add an object and an infinitive.
home-25.compare: English "I hear the birds singing" uses an -ing form; Dutch uses a bare infinitive after the object: de vogels zingen.

mistake.right: Ik hoor elke ochtend de vogels zingen.

leisure-15.meaning: Saying you are tired of this music.

conversation-58.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (vind) second (verb-second order).

mistake.why: The adjective goes after the object.

leisure-16.meaning: Saying you used to go to the park.
leisure-16.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ging) second (verb-second order).

leisure-16.compare: English "I used to go to the park" uses used to; Dutch uses the simple past ging with vroeger.

mistake.right: Ik ging vroeger naar het park.

school-17.meaning: Saying you learn something new every day.

mistake.wrong: Ik leer elke dag iets nieuw.
mistake.right: Ik leer elke dag iets nieuws.
mistake.why: After iets the adjective takes -s.

conversation-59.meaning: Saying she will believe in herself more.

mistake.right: Ze gaat meer in zichzelf geloven.

health-07.meaning: Saying she woke up and felt much better.

conversation-60.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-60.compare: English "He is very tall" is the same pattern; Dutch lang means both long and tall.

mistake.why: After zijn the adjective takes no -e ending.

home-26.meaning: Saying he washes his clothes at the laundrette.

leisure-17.meaning: Saying bowling is a fun social activity.

mistake.right: Bowlen is een leuke sociale activiteit.

conversation-61.meaning: Saying he called you this morning.

conversation-61.forms: Bellen: belde. Me is the object form of ik.
conversation-61.compare: English "He called me this morning." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: After a verb the pronoun takes its object form: me, not ik.

conversation-62.meaning: Saying you will be back in a moment.
conversation-62.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-62.forms: Zo here means in a moment.
conversation-62.compare: English "I will be right back" uses will; Dutch uses the present: ik ben zo terug.

transport-32.meaning: Saying he goes to work by bus.
transport-32.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order).
transport-32.forms: Gaan: hij gaat. Met plus a vehicle means by.
transport-32.compare: English "by bus" uses by; Dutch uses met de bus (with the bus).

mistake.wrong: Hij gaat door de bus naar zijn werk.
mistake.right: Hij gaat met de bus naar zijn werk.
mistake.why: To travel by a vehicle Dutch says met: met de bus.

leisure-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zingen) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
leisure-18.forms: Haar means her before a noun.
leisure-18.compare: English "Singing is her passion" uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive zingen as the subject.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

transport-33.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (gaan) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (weg) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-33.compare: English "We are leaving now" uses a progressive and one verb; Dutch splits weggaan: we gaan nu weg.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

leisure-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zingen) goes to the end.
leisure-19.forms: Zijn aan het plus infinitive shows an action in progress.
leisure-19.compare: English "She is singing now" uses -ing; Dutch uses is aan het zingen.

mistake.right: Ze is nu aan het zingen.
mistake.why: The progressive is aan het plus an infinitive; het cannot be left out.

leisure-20.meaning: Saying drawing is a creative hobby.
leisure-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Tekenen) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
leisure-20.forms: Hobby is a de-word, so creatieve takes -e.
leisure-20.compare: English "Drawing is a creative hobby" uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive tekenen as the subject.

mistake.why: After een a de-word takes -e.

home-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (meet) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-27.compare: English "I will measure it" uses will and no particle; Dutch uses the present and splits opmeten: ik meet het op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

conversation-63.meaning: Asking if someone will show it to you.
conversation-63.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Laat), and the subject (je) follows it. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zien) goes to the end.
conversation-63.forms: Laten zien means to show. The -t drops after je.
conversation-63.compare: English "Will you show it to me?" also starts with the verb; Dutch likewise puts the finite verb first, then the subject.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

food-14.meaning: Saying she likes cooking for her friends.
food-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (kookt) second (verb-second order).
food-14.forms: Graag after a verb means like to.
food-14.compare: English "She likes cooking" uses like plus -ing; Dutch uses the verb plus graag: ze kookt graag.

mistake.wrong: Ze kookt voor haar vrienden graag.
mistake.right: Ze kookt graag voor haar vrienden.
mistake.why: Graag comes right after the verb.

conversation-64.meaning: Telling someone they are free to go.
conversation-64.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (bent) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te gaan) closes the sentence.
conversation-64.forms: Vrij zijn om te means to be free to.
conversation-64.compare: English "You are free to go" uses to; Dutch needs om te: vrij om te gaan.

mistake.right: Je bent vrij om te gaan.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive after this adjective.

food-15.meaning: Saying she waited in the restaurant for an hour.
food-15.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (zitten) goes to the end; the infinitive (wachten) goes to the end.
food-15.forms: Zitten wachten means to wait (while sitting).
food-15.compare: English "She waited" is one verb; Dutch says heeft ... zitten wachten (has sat waiting).

mistake.wrong: Ze heeft een uur in het restaurant gezeten wachten.
mistake.right: Ze heeft een uur in het restaurant zitten wachten.
mistake.why: Use the infinitive zitten, not a participle.

conversation-65.meaning: Saying he gave you good advice.
conversation-65.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (gaf) second (verb-second order).
conversation-65.forms: Geven: gaf. Advies is a het-word, so goed has no -e.
conversation-65.compare: English "He gave me good advice." is also a simple past; Dutch forms it with -de/-te (regular) or a changed stem (irregular), and the plural ends in -den/-ten or -en.

mistake.why: Advies is a het-word: no -e after goed.

work-24.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (werk) comes second and the subject (je) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
work-24.forms: The -t drops after je: werk je.
work-24.compare: English "Where do you work?" needs do; Dutch just inverts: waar werk je?

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

home-28.meaning: Saying you will lift it up.
home-28.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (til) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-28.compare: English "I will lift it up" has up after the object; Dutch splits optillen: ik til het op.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

conversation-66.meaning: Saying it is better to help.
conversation-66.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om te helpen) closes the sentence.
conversation-66.forms: Beter is the comparative of goed.
conversation-66.compare: English "It is better to help." uses "to" or an -ing form; Dutch needs te (usually om ... te) before the infinitive.

mistake.right: Het is beter om te helpen.
mistake.why: Add om te before the infinitive after this adjective.

weather-12.meaning: Asking what the weather is like.
weather-12.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat voor weer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
weather-12.forms: Wat voor asks what kind of.
weather-12.compare: English "What is the weather like?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-16.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Heeft), and the subject (iemand) follows it.
food-16.forms: Iemand takes a singular verb: heeft.
food-16.compare: English "Does anyone have water?" needs "does" to form the question; Dutch just starts with the finite verb (Heeft).

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

school-18.meaning: Saying she explained it to you.
school-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (heeft) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (uitgelegd) goes to the end.
school-18.compare: English "She explained it to me." uses the simple past; Dutch often uses the perfect (auxiliary plus participle) for a finished event, with the participle (uitgelegd) at the end.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

weather-13.meaning: Saying she was looking at the sky.
weather-13.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (keek) second (verb-second order).
weather-13.compare: English "She was looking at the sky" is a past progressive; Dutch uses the simple past keek, followed by naar.

mistake.why: Kijken needs naar before what you look at.

shopping-22.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de prijs) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
shopping-22.compare: English "What is the price?" has the same order; Dutch prijs is a de-word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

conversation-67.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Is), and the subject (het) follows it.
conversation-67.compare: English "Is it safe?" has the same inversion; Dutch just moves is to the front.

mistake.why: A yes/no question starts with the finite verb, before the subject.

work-25.meaning: Saying you solve problems as soon as they arise.
work-25.order: The main clause has the verb second. After zodra the clause is subordinate, so the verb goes to the end.
work-25.compare: English "as soon as they arise" keeps the verb near the subject.

mistake.why: After zodra the verb goes to the end.

conversation-68.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dit) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order).
conversation-68.compare: English "This is my husband" has the same pattern; Dutch echtgenoot is a formal word for husband.

mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

health-08.meaning: Saying he follows a healthy diet.
health-08.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (volgt) second (verb-second order).
health-08.forms: Dieet is a het-word, so gezond has no -e.
health-08.compare: English "He follows a healthy diet." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: A het-word after een: no -e.

leisure-21.meaning: Saying they are talking about the film.
leisure-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (praten) second (verb-second order).
leisure-21.compare: English "They are talking about the film" is a progressive; Dutch uses the simple present: ze praten over de film.

mistake.why: Use over before the topic.

conversation-69.meaning: Saying you lose your patience when people are rude.
conversation-69.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (verlies) second (verb-second order). After als the clause is subordinate, so its finite verb (zijn) moves to the very end.
conversation-69.compare: English "when people are rude" keeps are near people.

mistake.why: After als the verb goes to the end.

conversation-70.meaning: Saying you are afraid of the future.
conversation-70.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (ben) second (verb-second order).
conversation-70.compare: English "afraid of" uses of; Dutch uses bang voor (afraid for).

mistake.wrong: Ik ben bang van de toekomst.
mistake.right: Ik ben bang voor de toekomst.
mistake.why: Bang zijn voor means to be afraid of: the preposition is voor.

conversation-71.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (het probleem) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
conversation-71.compare: English "What is the problem?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

transport-34.meaning: Saying you stand at the bus stop every morning.
transport-34.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (sta) second (verb-second order).
transport-34.compare: English "I stand at the bus stop every morning." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Ik staat elke ochtend bij de bushalte.
mistake.right: Ik sta elke ochtend bij de bushalte.
mistake.why: With ik the verb has no ending: ik sta.

work-26.meaning: Saying she will find a new job soon.
work-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vinden) goes to the end. Gaan plus an infinitive expresses a plan or something about to happen.
work-26.forms: Nieuwe takes -e before the de-word baan.
work-26.compare: English "She is going to find a new job soon".

mistake.wrong: Ze gaat binnenkort vinden een nieuwe baan.
mistake.right: Ze gaat binnenkort een nieuwe baan vinden.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

school-19.meaning: Saying she did not go to school.
school-19.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Zij) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegaan) goes to the end.
school-19.compare: English "She did not go to school" uses "did not"; Dutch uses the perfect with zijn and niet: is niet naar school gegaan.

mistake.wrong: Zij heeft niet naar school gegaan.
mistake.right: Zij is niet naar school gegaan.
mistake.why: Gaan is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses zijn.

leisure-22.meaning: Saying you used to go to the beach every summer.
leisure-22.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Wij) comes first and the finite verb (gingen) second (verb-second order).
leisure-22.compare: English "We used to go" uses used to; Dutch uses the simple past gingen with vroeger.

mistake.wrong: Wij gaan vroeger elke zomer naar het strand.
mistake.right: Wij gingen vroeger elke zomer naar het strand.
mistake.why: With vroeger Dutch uses the simple past: gingen.

conversation-72.meaning: Saying it is hard to say.
conversation-72.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Het) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the te phrase (te zeggen) closes the sentence.
conversation-72.compare: English "It is hard to say" has the same shape; Dutch needs te before the infinitive.

mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive after this adjective.

home-29.meaning: Saying you had already cleaned the house.
home-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (schoongemaakt) goes to the end.
home-29.compare: English "We had already cleaned the house." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (schoongemaakt) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: We hadden schoongemaakt het huis al.
mistake.right: We hadden het huis al schoongemaakt.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

conversation-73.meaning: Saying you had already checked the time.
conversation-73.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gecontroleerd) goes to the end.
conversation-73.compare: English "I had already checked the time." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (gecontroleerd) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gecontroleerd de tijd al.
mistake.right: Ik had de tijd al gecontroleerd.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

shopping-23.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Dat) comes first and the finite verb (lijkt) second (verb-second order).
shopping-23.forms: Lijken op means to look like.
shopping-23.compare: English "That looks like gold" uses like; Dutch uses lijken op.

mistake.why: Lijken op means to look like: the preposition op is required.

home-30.meaning: Saying walking the dog is your job.
home-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De hond uitlaten) comes first and the finite verb (is) second (verb-second order). An infinitive can be the whole subject.
home-30.forms: Uitlaten stays whole at the end of the phrase.
home-30.compare: English "Walking the dog" uses an -ing noun; Dutch uses the infinitive phrase de hond uitlaten.

mistake.wrong: De hond uitlaten is taak mijn.
mistake.right: De hond uitlaten is mijn taak.
mistake.why: The possessive comes before the noun.

work-27.meaning: Saying they will start building next month.

parts.label: preposition phrase
parts.text: met de bouw van het nieuwe gebouw

work-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (beginnen) second (verb-second order).
work-27.forms: Beginnen met. Nieuwe takes -e after het with the article.
work-27.compare: English "They will start constructing" uses will; Dutch uses the present tense for a plan: ze beginnen volgende maand.

mistake.wrong: Ze beginnen volgende maand de bouw.
mistake.right: Ze beginnen volgende maand met de bouw.
mistake.why: Beginnen needs met before the activity that starts.

home-31.meaning: Saying you did not make a mess of it.
home-31.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Je) comes first and the finite verb (hebt) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gemaakt) goes to the end.
home-31.forms: Er een puinhoop van maken means to make a mess of it.
home-31.compare: English "You did not make a mess of it" uses "did not"; Dutch uses the perfect: hebt er geen puinhoop van gemaakt.

mistake.wrong: Je hebt er niet een puinhoop van gemaakt.
mistake.right: Je hebt er geen puinhoop van gemaakt.
mistake.why: Use geen instead of niet een before a noun.

health-09.order: This is a yes/no question. With no question word, it begins with the finite verb (Voel), and the subject (je) follows it.
health-09.forms: Zich voelen: the reflexive je is repeated after the subject je.
health-09.compare: English "Do you feel better?" uses do and no reflexive; Dutch repeats je: voel je je beter?

mistake.why: Voelen needs the reflexive pronoun.

school-20.meaning: Saying they will understand the rules after the training.
school-20.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (zullen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (begrijpen) goes to the end.
school-20.compare: English "They will understand the rules after the training".

mistake.wrong: Ze zullen begrijpen de regels na de training.
mistake.right: Ze zullen de regels begrijpen na de training.
mistake.why: The object comes before the infinitive.

administration-05.meaning: Asking how long the wait is.
administration-05.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (de wachttijd) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject.
administration-05.compare: English "How long is the wait?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: In a question the verb comes before the subject.

food-17.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
food-17.forms: Dorst hebben means to be thirsty.
food-17.compare: English "I am thirsty" uses am; Dutch uses have.

mistake.why: Dutch says ik heb dorst (I have thirst), not ik ben dorst.

conversation-74.meaning: Saying she heard the news on the radio.
conversation-74.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hoorde) second (verb-second order).
conversation-74.compare: English "She heard the news" is the same simple past; Dutch nieuws is a het-word and singular.

mistake.wrong: Ze hoorde de nieuws op de radio.
mistake.right: Ze hoorde het nieuws op de radio.
mistake.why: Nieuws is a het-word, so the article is het.

shopping-24.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order).
shopping-24.compare: English "I need my wallet" is one verb; Dutch splits ik heb ... nodig around the object.

mistake.why: Nodig goes after the object.

food-18.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hadden) second (verb-second order).
food-18.compare: English "They did not have any water" needs "did not"; Dutch simply says ze hadden geen water.

mistake.why: Use geen instead of niet before a noun.

home-32.meaning: Saying they will hang up the decorations this afternoon.
home-32.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (hangen) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-32.compare: English "They will hang up the decorations" keeps up beside the verb; Dutch splits ophangen: ze hangen ... op.

mistake.right: Ze hangen vanmiddag de versieringen op.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

conversation-75.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (probeer) second (verb-second order).
conversation-75.compare: English "I will try again" uses will; Dutch uses the present tense: ik probeer het opnieuw.

mistake.why: The object comes before opnieuw.

transport-35.meaning: Saying she is going to fly to London next summer.
transport-35.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gaat) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (vliegen) goes to the end. Gaan plus an infinitive expresses a plan or something about to happen.
transport-35.compare: English "She is going to fly" uses going to; Dutch uses gaan plus an infinitive at the end: ze gaat ... vliegen.

mistake.wrong: Ze gaat vliegen volgende zomer naar Londen.
mistake.right: Ze gaat volgende zomer naar Londen vliegen.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

school-21.meaning: Saying you knew the answer but forgot it.
school-21.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wist) second (verb-second order). Maar joins two main clauses, so each keeps its own verb second.
school-21.compare: English "I knew the answer, but I have forgotten it." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (vergeten) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ik wist het antwoord, maar ik heb het vergeten.
mistake.right: Ik wist het antwoord, maar ik ben het vergeten.
mistake.why: The usual perfect of vergeten uses zijn: ik ben het vergeten.

work-28.meaning: Saying you write reports every week.
work-28.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (schrijven) second (verb-second order).
work-28.compare: English "We write reports every week" has the same pattern; Dutch puts the time phrase before the object.

mistake.why: With we the verb ends in -en.

transport-36.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wanneer) takes the first position, so the finite verb (komen) comes second and the subject (ze) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (aan) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
transport-36.compare: English "When will they arrive?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

work-29.meaning: Saying you are thinking about changing jobs.
work-29.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (denk) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the om te phrase (om van baan te veranderen) closes the sentence.
work-29.forms: Van baan veranderen means to change jobs.
work-29.compare: English "I am thinking about changing jobs" uses -ing; Dutch uses om ... te plus an infinitive: erover om van baan te veranderen.

mistake.wrong: Ik denk erover om van baan veranderen.
mistake.right: Ik denk erover om van baan te veranderen.
mistake.why: Put te before the infinitive.

conversation-76.meaning: Asking what kind of noise that is.
conversation-76.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Wat) takes the first position, so the finite verb (is) comes second and the subject (dat) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. Wat is dat voor ... asks what kind of something it is.
conversation-76.compare: English "What is that noise?" has a similar order; Dutch also puts the finite verb straight after the question word.

mistake.why: Keep dat after the verb and voor geluid together.

transport-37.order: This is a question. The question word or phrase (Waar) takes the first position, so the finite verb (zijn) comes second and the subject (ze) follows it: question word + finite verb + subject. The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gegaan) goes to the end.
transport-37.compare: English "Where did they go?" uses did; Dutch uses the perfect with zijn: waar zijn ze heen gegaan?

mistake.why: Gaan is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses zijn.

home-33.meaning: Saying you will tidy your room before you leave.
home-33.order: The main clause uses gaan plus an infinitive. After voordat the verb goes to the end.
home-33.forms: Weggaan is one word when the verb is at the end.
home-33.compare: English "before you leave" keeps the verb in the middle; Dutch sends it to the end: voordat je weggaat.

mistake.why: A separable verb at the end is one word.

conversation-77.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (leek) second (verb-second order).
conversation-77.compare: English "She seemed confused." has the same basic pattern; in Dutch the adjective takes no ending after a form of zijn or worden.

mistake.why: After a linking verb such as klinken or lijken the adjective takes no -e ending.

home-34.meaning: Saying you grow your own vegetables in the garden.
home-34.order: In a normal main clause the subject (We) comes first and the finite verb (kweken) second (verb-second order).
home-34.compare: English "our own vegetables" puts own after our; Dutch does the same: onze eigen groenten.

mistake.why: Eigen comes after the possessive.

shopping-25.meaning: Saying you sold your old car last month.
shopping-25.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (heb) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (verkocht) goes to the end.
shopping-25.forms: Verkopen: verkocht. Oude takes -e before the de-word auto.
shopping-25.compare: English "I sold my old car" is a simple past; Dutch uses the perfect: ik heb ... verkocht.

mistake.wrong: Ik heb vorige maand mijn oud auto verkocht.
mistake.right: Ik heb vorige maand mijn oude auto verkocht.
mistake.why: After a possessive a de-word takes -e.

conversation-78.meaning: Saying you want to know why.
conversation-78.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (wil) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (weten) goes to the end.
conversation-78.compare: English "I want to know why" has the same order; Dutch waarom closes the clause.

mistake.why: Weten comes before the question word.

transport-38.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (kwamen) second (verb-second order).
transport-38.compare: English "They arrived late" is one verb; Dutch says kwamen te laat (came too late).

mistake.why: The past plural of komen is kwamen.

shopping-26.meaning: Saying you had already done the shopping.
shopping-26.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (had) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the participle (gedaan) goes to the end.
shopping-26.forms: Boodschappen doen means to do the shopping.
shopping-26.compare: English "I had already done the shopping." also uses an auxiliary plus a participle, but keeps the participle next to the auxiliary; Dutch puts the participle (gedaan) at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ik had gedaan de boodschappen al.
mistake.right: Ik had de boodschappen al gedaan.
mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

home-35.meaning: Promising to repair it for someone.
home-35.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (zal) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the infinitive (repareren) goes to the end.
home-35.compare: English "I will repair it for you." keeps the second verb next to the modal; Dutch sends the infinitive (repareren) to the end of the clause.

mistake.wrong: Ik zal repareren het voor je.
mistake.right: Ik zal het voor je repareren.
mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end.

weather-14.order: In a normal main clause the subject (De herfst) comes first and the finite verb (komt) second (verb-second order).
weather-14.compare: English "Autumn is coming" is the same idea; Dutch adds eraan: de herfst komt eraan.

mistake.why: Add eraan for approaching.

shopping-27.meaning: Saying he stands behind the counter in the bakery.
shopping-27.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Hij) comes first and the finite verb (staat) second (verb-second order).
shopping-27.compare: English "He stands behind the counter in the bakery." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.why: The preposition comes before its noun.

work-30.meaning: Saying you start working at eight in the morning.
work-30.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (begin) second (verb-second order).
work-30.compare: English "I start work at eight in the morning." has the same basic order: subject, then verb, then the rest.

mistake.wrong: Ik begin om acht uur 's ochtends werken.
mistake.right: Ik begin om acht uur 's ochtends met werken.
mistake.why: Beginnen needs met before the activity that starts.

conversation-79.order: A fixed expression with no finite verb: an adverb followed by a participle (short for ik heb het graag gedaan).
conversation-79.forms: Short for ik heb het graag gedaan.
conversation-79.compare: English "You're welcome" is a different phrase; Dutch graag gedaan literally means "gladly done".

mistake.why: Graag gedaan is a fixed phrase with nothing added.

home-36.meaning: Saying you make your bed every morning.
home-36.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ik) comes first and the finite verb (maak) second (verb-second order). The other verb parts are not conjugated: the separable particle (op) goes to the end while the verb itself stays second.
home-36.compare: English "I make my bed" has no particle; Dutch opmaken splits: ik maak ... op.

mistake.wrong: Ik opmaak elke ochtend mijn bed.
mistake.right: Ik maak elke ochtend mijn bed op.
mistake.why: A separable verb splits in a main clause: the verb stays second and the particle goes to the end.

home-37.meaning: Saying they use the leftover paint for the bedroom.
home-37.order: In a normal main clause the subject (Ze) comes first and the finite verb (gebruiken) second (verb-second order).
home-37.forms: Overgebleven is a participle used as an adjective.
home-37.compare: English "the leftover paint" uses leftover; Dutch uses the participle overgebleven as an adjective.

mistake.why: The adjective comes between the article and the noun.
